Hitmen Rollo and Marcus drove across the city, debating foreign drug laws and the peculiar names given to fast food abroad. Outside their target’s flat, they argued in the corridor whether giving a man’s wife a foot massage justified being thrown from a balcony. Moments later, Marcus recited a passage of scripture before he and Rollo shot young Tobin for double-crossing their employer, Otis, and retrieved a silver briefcase. Before they could leave, a fourth man concealed in the bathroom burst out, emptying a revolver at them from six feet away; every bullet buried itself harmlessly in the wall, an outcome Marcus instantly termed divine intervention.

In the getaway car, Rollo’s gun accidentally discharged over a bump, blowing away their back-seat passenger Del. Bloodied and compromised, Marcus parked at his friend Warren’s house, where a soft-spoken fixer coordinated a precise cleanup, hosing them down in the yard and dressing them in borrowed shorts and T-shirts. Afterwards, over breakfast in a coffee shop, two small-time robbers decided on a whim to hold up the diner. Mid-holdup, Marcus talked the male robber down, recited his scripture once more, handed over his wallet but kept the briefcase, and allowed the couple to walk out free. Later that evening, Rollo bought pure heroin from his dealer Kip and shot up at the kitchen table. He then escorted Otis’s wife, Nadia, to a themed diner where they took off their shoes and won a dance contest. But back at the flat, Nadia snorted Rollo’s heroin thinking it was cocaine; she overdosed, going blue on the carpet, until Rollo brought her back with a needle of adrenaline driven into her heart on Kip’s living-room floor.

***

Years earlier, a returning prisoner of war sat a young boy named Denny down in a bare front room, placing into his small hands the gold watch his father had kept hidden through years of captivity.

Decades later, two hitmen wearing borrowed shorts and T-shirts delivered a briefcase to Otis at his bar, where Otis was busy counting out cash to the aging boxer Denny, paying him to take a dive in the fifth round. Denny took the money, but he did not go down. He fought to win, striking his opponent hard enough to kill him in the ring, before fleeing the arena in a passing taxi.

Hiding in a motel on the edge of town with his girlfriend Marielle, Denny discovered she had forgotten his father's watch on his flat's bedside table. Refusing to leave it behind, Denny returned to the watched apartment and found the timepiece. As he stood at the kitchen counter, Rollo emerged from the bathroom—but Denny snatched a submachine gun resting on the counter first and shot Rollo dead.

Driving away, Denny collided with Otis in the street as his employer crossed in front of his bonnet with a paper bag in his arms. Both wrecked their cars and were dragged down into the basement of a pawnshop by its owners. Denny broke free from his restraints and reached the street door, but stopped and turned back. Grabbing a sword off the pawnshop wall, he went back down and saved Otis while one of their captors was raping him. Declared square by a stunned Otis on the condition that he never set foot in the city again, Denny collected Marielle, mounted a motorcycle taken from the pawnshop, and rode out into the night with his father’s watch back on his wrist.

The robbery collapsed within a minute. Police sirens wailed as Mr. Ash fired through the windshield to clear a path from the getaway car. On foot, Mr. Elm hijacked a sedan, but the terrified driver pulled a pistol from her door pocket and shot him in the stomach. Elm killed her, grabbed the wheel, and bled out until Ash found him, drove him screaming to the warehouse rendezvous, and cradled him on the concrete, swearing he was not going to die.

Months before the blood ran, Pruitt had coached undercover officer Danny Roarke in a windowless room, forcing him to rehearse a fabricated anecdote about a drug bust in a public toilet until he could tell it like a true memory. Danny performed the story in a bar for the boss Bram, his son Cal, and Ash, successfully earning his way onto the crew as Mr. Elm.

Inside the warehouse, Mr. Birch arrived clean and furious, arguing that the job was an inside setup with an informer present. Birch stepped outside and hid the diamonds where no one watching could find them.

Earlier that morning, Ren Vasco had walked out of prison and reported straight to Bram and Cal, who owed him for the years he had kept his mouth shut. Afterward, the crew argued over breakfast about what a pop song was really about and whether waitresses deserved tips, right before Bram handed out the tree aliases over Birch's loud objections to being called Mr. Birch.

Now Ren strolled into the warehouse, dragging a kidnapped patrolman named Doyle from the boot of his car. Left alone with the officer, Ren turned up an oldie on the radio, danced a few steps, sliced off Doyle's ear with a razor, and doused him in petrol.

From the floor, Elm summoned his strength and shot Ren dead. Elm whispered to Doyle that he was a cop and that police were waiting outside for Bram. But Cal returned, listened to Elm's story, and put three rounds into Doyle himself to eliminate the witness.

Bram arrived moments later, looked at Elm, and flatly named him as the informer. Ash refused to believe it, turning his gun on Bram to protect Elm. The three-way standoff exploded into gunfire. Bram and Cal collapsed dead onto the floor, leaving only Ash and Elm breathing.

Bleeding out, Elm confessed to Ash that he was indeed a police officer. Heartbroken, Ash put his gun to Elm's head and fired just as the police stormed the warehouse, cutting Ash down in a hail of bullets.

On his twenty-fifth birthday, Emmett Rusk claimed his inheritance from the banker Barrow and demanded control of a single holding: the failing city newspaper, the Clarion, simply because he thought it would be fun. He moved a bed directly into the office, installed his manager Marsh and his friend Devlin on either side of him, and printed a signed statement of principles across the front page. To ensure victory, Emmett bought out the rival paper’s entire staff with exorbitant salaries and threw a lavish party complete with a brass band and a dancing chorus line.

Years before, in a western mining boarding house, Emmett’s mother had sat at a kitchen table signing her son and their new fortune over to Barrow after a defaulted lodger’s mine deed yielded an enormous vein of ore, ignoring her husband’s bitter protests from the doorway. 

Returning from a European buying trip, Emmett announced his engagement to Adele, the governor’s niece. The marriage quickly withered into silence across an endless breakfast table behind separate newspapers. Then a passing cab splattered mud on Emmett’s coat outside a chemist, and his shared laughter with a shopgirl named Nora Kell began a series of secret evening visits to her rooms.

During Emmett’s campaign for governor, political boss Halloran brought Adele straight to Nora’s door, threatening public exposure unless Emmett withdrew. Emmett told him to get out. He lost the election, printed claims of polling fraud, transferred Devlin to another city, and watched his marriage quietly collapse. 

Emmett married Nora next, forcing her into an opera career despite her utter lack of voice. Her debut was a disaster. Devlin, brought back to cover it, got drunk and collapsed over a savage review; Emmett finished the brutal text himself, printed it, and fired his friend. Nora swallowed poison in a dark room rather than face another audience, and only then did Emmett permit her to stop singing.

He locked her away in the vast, drafty palace of Silvermount, where she passed empty days completing jigsaw puzzles on the hall floor.

When they had come down the boarding house steps long ago to take the boy east, young Emmett had driven his sled into Barrow’s stomach with enough force to knock the banker down, though they dragged him away regardless.

At Silvermount, a miserable beach picnic ended in a heated argument, prompting Nora to pack her bags and leave. Enraged, Emmett wrecked her bedroom until his fingers closed around a glass snow globe. He whispered "Bluebell" and walked past endless facing mirrors that multiplied his aging figure into infinity.

In his grand bedroom, Emmett died alone, murmuring "Bluebell" as the glass globe fell from his hand and shattered on the floor. 

A newsreel obituary recapped his public triumphs and scandals but offered no explanation for his final word. Sent to solve the mystery, reporter Nash was promptly thrown out by a drunk Nora in a seaside nightclub. Nash scoured Barrow’s memoirs and interviewed Marsh, Devlin, Nora, and the old butler Colm. Ultimately, Nash closed his notebook, concluding that no single word could ever unlock a man's life—unaware that down in the cellars of Silvermount, workmen clearing out crates were throwing a small wooden sled marked *Bluebell* directly into the furnace.

Working behind an insurance desk, Martin Kray put Elias Prine through ruthless evaluations, writing off the claimant’s severe memory loss as psychosomatic and denying the claim. Unable to believe her husband’s condition, Elias’s diabetic wife tested him by asking for injection after injection; Elias gave each one as if for the first time, killing her with an overdose he could not remember administering.

In a derelict basement, a dying man named Gil Marsh choked out a final whisper—"Elias"—that Martin couldn't explain. Ignoring the word, Martin stripped Gil’s suit onto his own back, pocketed his keys, and drove off in the dead man’s sports car. At her bar, Gil’s girlfriend Corinne instantly recognized her missing partner’s clothes and vehicle, serving Martin a beer her staff had secretly spat in.

Two intruders crashed into Martin’s bathroom late at night. Martin shot one across his wife’s lifeless body, but the second attacker smashed his head into the bathroom mirror, leaving Martin permanently unable to form new memories. To function, Martin constructed a rigorous system of instant photographs, annotated notes, and permanent tattoos to hunt the missing killer known only as R.M.

Corinne hid every pen in her house, then goaded Martin until he hit her. Stepping outside until purple bruises rose, she returned to accuse a man named Vance, knowing Martin’s memory system made him an easily pointed weapon. Martin ambushed Vance in a motel bathroom, savagely beating him and driving him out of town at gunpoint.

A year before, plainclothes officer Roy had helped Martin track down and shoot the real attacker in an abandoned building, an act of vengeance Martin forgot within minutes. Unaware it was over, Martin stood in a quiet field burning his dead wife's hairbrush and paperbacks, trying to grieve a loss his mind could never retain long enough to heal.

In the derelict building, Roy finally sat Martin down and laid out the truth: Gil Marsh was innocent, Martin’s real revenge had happened a year ago, and the tragic Prine case Martin recited to strangers was actually his own buried history. Refusing to accept a truth that left him without purpose, Martin burned his photographs of Gil, wrote *he is lying to you* across Roy’s picture, and copied Roy's license plate as his new target.

In a room he didn't remember renting, Martin sat on the bed speaking into the telephone, narrating the Prine case to an anonymous listener. The caller fed Martin a name, trade, and location, identifying drug dealer Gil Marsh as his wife's killer.

Martin walked into a tattoo parlor with a slip of paper and had Roy's license plate etched into his thigh as his sixth unquestioned fact. Days later, Corinne ran that tattooed plate through a contact at the vehicle registry and handed Martin an official record naming Roy Mercer.

Tracking Gil Marsh to a wet basement, Martin beat the dealer and strangled him with a belt. He snapped a photograph of the corpse, satisfied that justice was done.

Martin lured Roy out to the derelict building on a lie, walked him into the shadowed hallway, and shot him through the head. He snapped a photo of Roy's body, completely confident in the note he had written to himself.

Tobias woke with a hollow ache behind his eyes and no memory of how he’d lost yesterday. His apartment felt strangely vast, stripped of an echo he couldn’t name. He knew only the quiet geometry of his own life, exactly as it had been two years prior.

Long before that emptiness, Tobias had met Ivy at the end of the rail line on a cold beach. They had smashed the window of an abandoned shore house to sleep on bare floorboards. For two years, warmth lived in small spaces: skating across frozen river ice, steam on noodle house windows, low audio at drive-in movies. But love curdled. Her drinking turned to armor; his silence became an accusation. When she drove his car into a post at two in the morning, their furious row severed them completely, and Ivy walked out for good.

On an unexplainable impulse, Tobias skipped work and boarded a train heading east. He walked onto the frozen sand, where a woman with dyed hair stood shivering against the wind. When she turned, her eyes held no recognition, yet they stood together as if drawn by a tide.

Desperate to escape the pain after walking out, Ivy had paid a clinic to scrub Tobias from her mind entirely. Days later, Tobias had tracked her to a bookshop, only to find her looking straight through him, flirting with a young clerk named Peck. Devastated, Tobias had been shown the clinic’s form letter by his friends Nina and Grady. Driven by grief, he confronted Dr. Hallam, demanded the same procedure, and filled two carrier bags with her hairslide, a favorite mug, and paper scraps so the mapping could begin.

Driving back to the city from the coast, conversation flowed between Tobias and Ivy with unearned intimacy. Outside her building, Ivy invited him up for a drink, as if continuing a conversation started long ago.

That night in Tobias’s flat, technicians Dell and Peck had attached the memory cap while he slept. Peck quietly pocketed the bagged keepsakes, intending to use them on Ivy himself. Deep inside his own head, Tobias watched their final, ugliest fights dissolve into grey dust. But as the deletion swept backward into the golden months on the ice, regret seized him. Desperate, Tobias grabbed her memory-self, dragging Ivy into places she’d never been—under his childhood dining table, hidden behind forgotten schoolyards—to save her from the map.

In her stairwell weeks later, two thick manila envelopes lay on the threshold. Rosa, the clinic receptionist, had quit and mailed every patient their original tapes and case files. Together, Tobias and Ivy pressed play, sitting side-by-side as their recorded past selves tore each other apart in brutal, unforgiving detail. Ivy gasped and ran down the steps, but stopped at the landing. She walked back up, sat beside him, and they agreed to try anyway.

Hours before that choice, Dell and Rosa had gotten high on Tobias’s bed, ignoring the monitor as his mental map spiraled off course. Dr. Hallam was summoned at three in the morning to restore control. When Rosa impulsively kissed Hallam in the hallway, his arriving wife coldly informed the receptionist that her own affair with the doctor had been systematically erased months ago. Hallam reset the machinery, driving the deletion to its final node: the abandoned shore house from the night Tobias and Ivy first met. As the room dissolved around them, Ivy looked at Tobias one last time and whispered a instruction to meet her on the beach.

In a motel doorway, an ex-convict stands bleeding through his shirt, asking to be finished. The man holding the pistol turns the barrel against his own chest instead and pulls the trigger. In the car, someone holds the horn down all the way to the emergency room, but on the operating table, the transplanted heart fails completely. Afterwards, Lena Ward goes home alone, pregnant with a child, while the wounded ex-convict returns to the wife and family he had once walked out on.

In a suburban house, Lena lives a settled life—sober for years, keeping the garden, raising two young daughters with her husband Doug. In a hospital side room off a corridor, a doctor tells her that Doug and both girls are dead. At a kitchen table where her daughters’ drawings still hang on the wall, Lena cuts lines of white powder, starting up again in locked bar bathrooms and methodically destroying herself with cocaine.

A mathematician named Aaron Vale sits in a cardiology clinic as a doctor shows him numbers, explaining that his failing heart leaves him mere weeks to live unless a donor dies at the right time. Somewhere in the same building, a surgeon opens his chest, transplanting a dead man's heart into Aaron so he wakes up alive and able to breathe for the first time in months. In a dark car park, Aaron pays a private investigator to break the rules and find the name and street of the donor’s widow.

Wes Tarrow, a born-again ex-convict with scripture inked up both forearms, coaches boys’ baseball on Saturdays while his wife Nita watches his temper and fanaticism like bad weather gathering. A pickup truck comes through a crossing, taking a man and two children off their feet. The truck pauses a hundred yards off with the engine running, backs up a little, then flees. Wes walks up the steps of a police station on his own, confesses his hit-and-run to the desk sergeant, and is sent back to prison.

Aaron follows Lena, engineering meetings at a swimming pool until an affair begins. In his old house, Aaron tells his estranged wife Della that he is leaving and refuses to let her use his frozen sperm to conceive a child. Later, Aaron admits to Lena in her kitchen that her husband’s heart is beating in his chest. She throws him out into the night with his belongings, but four days later she takes him back.

Released early from prison, Wes walks past his family waiting at the gate, abandoning his faith to take work cleaning rooms at a motel four hundred miles away. Lena demands that Wes be killed, saying she cannot breathe sharing a country with him. Aaron buys a gun from a man in a lock-up and tracks Wes to the motel. He gets Wes against a wall in the dark behind the building, but cannot make his hand pull the trigger to kill; he merely wounds Wes and tells him to run.

Della sits across a kitchen table with a clinic form, pressing Aaron to agree to insemination before his heart kills him. Wes preaches to boys on the diamond. A truck strikes three people at a crossing. A heart passes from one chest to another. A widow falls back into addiction, a murderer seeks his own end, and three lives tangle without a beginning or an end.

Wes walks up the steps of a police station on his own, confesses his hit-and-run to the desk sergeant, and is sent back to prison.

Above the blare of sirens, an old man stood at an open window overlooking the street, explaining to a younger man that nothing anybody does survives time—and that this was not a complaint, merely a fact.

Below him, in a street bathed in pulsing blue light, police officers carried two men out through the gathering crowd. Hands cuffed behind their backs, one shouted blindly into the night while the other remained entirely silent.

Minutes earlier, inside the murky basement of the club, Jonah had snatched a heavy fire extinguisher off the wall and swung it repeatedly down into a man’s face, long after the body had stopped moving. A few feet away, standing quietly amidst the panicked crowd, watched the Adder—the real rapist, whom they had missed entirely.

Before the murder, Cort had hunted through the dark room, pulling faces out of the shadows until he picked one. But the man Cort grabbed seized his elbow and twisted it with brutal precision, snapping the arm where it stood.

Earlier still, in a narrow side street, two men had detached themselves from a dark doorway to offer Cort and Jonah a rapist's name and location in exchange for cash, steering them down toward the basement club called the Pit.

That frantic hunt had begun outside a flat party, where Cort and Jonah stepped out into the night air still half-laughing, only to freeze. In the street, paramedics were loading a bloody face onto a trolley under a blanket—Lise, being lifted into the back of an ambulance.

Hours before they found her, Lise had been trapped in a concrete pedestrian underpass. The Adder had turned his violence onto her without hurry, raping her and beating her head against the concrete floor, while a passer-by at the far end of the tunnel glimpsed the assault, hesitated, and backed away into the night.

She had descended those stairs only to avoid a busy road of four lanes of headlights, stepping into the tiled tunnel just as the pimp known as the Adder was holding a transsexual woman by her hair, explaining something to her with his fist.

She had been walking alone because Cort had spent the party getting steadily drunk and high, openly pursuing other women. Disgusted and quiet, Lise had collected her coat and left on her own.

Earlier that evening, they had been whole. Lise, Cort, and Jonah stood swaying together in an underground carriage, cheerfully arguing about sex and Cort’s drinking with the easy banter of people who fully expected to be arguing again tomorrow.

That afternoon had been untouched by any of it. Sprinklers turned lazily over cut grass in a public park as children ran through the spray. Lise lay on her side in the sun with a book she was not really reading, one hand resting flat against her stomach.

That morning, she had sat on the edge of the bath, alone in the flat, holding a small plastic stick in both hands. Finding that the pregnancy test was positive, she had let herself smile before she had told anyone at all.

And before the test, in the soft morning light filtering through thin curtains, Lise lay in bed beside Cort. She described a recurring dream of a red tunnel she kept walking into, while the two of them teased each other about her ex-boyfriend Jonah.

For six months of total insomnia, weeping in church halls into the shoulders of dying strangers was the only thing that brought sleep. Then Ada Vey started showing up, obvious in her faked grief, and her lie destroyed my sanctuary. On a business flight shortly after, I met a soap salesman named Rex Marrow, who gave me his card after a long tirade on consumerism.

Down a cold service stairwell beneath a financial tower, Rex beat me down flight after flight. The gun was in his hand—no, my hand—and the steel barrel tasted of oil and cold metal pressed hard against my tongue. I angled the barrel upward and pulled the trigger, shooting myself straight through the cheek to destroy the man who refused to let me go.

When my flight landed, an explosion had gutted my flat and reduced my catalogue furniture to ash. I called Rex from a street phone, and he brought me into a derelict house at the edge of the industrial district. Outside a bar that same week, he asked me to hit him as hard as I could, and we beat each other bloody on the wet car park tarmac.

What started as two men brawling hardened into a weekly basement club with its own rules, pulling in more and more members.

Ada overdosed one night, and Rex brought her back to the derelict house. Soon the two of them were engaged in a loud affair that echoed through the floorboards while I lay downstairs, unable to stand it. Between nights with Ada, Rex rendered fat stolen from a cosmetic surgery clinic yard into high-end soap on our kitchen stove, selling it back to department stores at eighty dollars a bar.

One afternoon, Rex held my wet hand flat on the kitchen table and poured chemical lye onto the back of it, burning me while refusing to let me retreat into meditation. Scarred and bruised, I walked into my employer’s office, smashed my face into the carpet, and blackmailed my boss into paying me to stay away.

With a steady salary and income from the soap, Rex turned the club into an organisation called Havoc, filling the house with shaven-headed recruits who took orders and vandalised corporate property. During a nighttime drive, Rex took his hands off the wheel, steered into oncoming traffic, let the car roll into a ditch, and vanished.

When a Havoc member named Ogden was shot dead on an operation, I started trying to shut the whole thing down. Travelling from city to city, I found identical cellar clubs everywhere, where barmen and strangers looked up and greeted me as Rex Marrow. 

In a motel room littered with travel receipts, I finally worked it out: Rex and I were the same person. Rex had been acting while I thought I was sleeping. I got Ada on the phone, and she confirmed she had been sleeping with me, not a separate man.

Tracing Havoc’s ultimate objective, I discovered that the organisation had mined the underground car parks of the towers holding the nation's debt records. As I searched beneath the buildings to defuse the charges, Rex materialized and dragged me down a service stairwell a flight at a time. At the bottom, realizing the gun was in my own fingers, I shoved the steel in my mouth and fired through my cheek to kill Rex.

Bleeding heavily, I was found by the shaven recruits, who delivered Ada up to the high window of the tower, apologised, and left. Ada took my hand, and together we watched from the window as the towers came down one by one.

Nadir stood at the glass counter while his daughter Sahar translated. The dealer sneered, mocking Nadir’s thick accent, but handed over the handgun anyway. 

Across town, Trey and Kwame stepped onto a restaurant pavement, pulled pistols, and carjacked prosecutor Halstead and his wife Paula. 

Later that night, Officer Boyle pulled over Clay and Renee Hobart for no real infraction. Boyle forced Renee against the bonnet, groping her under her skirt, while Clay stood frozen three feet away and Boyle’s partner, Officer Voss, watched in silent disgust.

Driving along a dark, deserted country road under heavy rain, Officer Voss pulled his cruiser over to pick up a young hitchhiker. They spoke softly for a mile until the young man reached into his coat pocket. Voss panicked, drew his sidearm, and shot Kwame twice in the chest. Staring at the harmless object slipping from the dead boy's hand, Voss drove the car into a ditch, set it ablaze, and fled.

The morning after the Hobart stop, Voss walked into his commander's office and begged for a new patrol car rather than keep riding with a racist. When offered a swap on the condition he blame his partner's flatulence, Voss accepted the lie just to get away.

Meanwhile, Mateo fitted new front-door locks at the Halstead residence. From the top of the stairs, Paula shouted loudly enough for Mateo to hear, telling her husband the tattooed locksmith would sell their keys to a gang by nightfall. Mateo finished silently, then went to Nadir’s shop. He replaced Nadir's lock, warning him that the door frame itself was broken and needed replacing. Nadir, convinced Mateo was running a con, threw him out.

That afternoon, Boyle sat across a desk from health insurance clerk Delia Frank, pleading for treatment for his father, who wept from pain whenever he passed water. Delia gave a flat refusal, and Boyle exploded at the name on her badge.

Overnight, thieves smashed Nadir’s shop door off its hinges, destroying his stock and writing on the walls. The insurance company reviewed the file and denied the claim because Nadir had ignored the locksmith's warning.

On a slip road, a wrecked car lay upside down with petrol leaking toward an open flame. Renee was trapped inside until Boyle crawled through the broken glass, cut her seatbelt, and pulled her out.

Elsewhere in Halstead's car, Trey and Kwame struck a small shopkeeper, Pham, crossing between parked vans. After arguing for two streets, they dumped the breathing man outside a hospital entrance.

Later, four officers surrounded Clay Hobart, believing his vehicle was stolen. As they drew their guns on him, Voss stepped into the middle, defused the situation, and saved Clay's life. Clay sped away from the scene with Trey crouched in his passenger seat, dropping the young man on a roadside verge three miles later.

Driven mad by his financial ruin, Nadir waited outside Mateo’s house with the pistol hidden in his coat. When Mateo emerged, his small daughter Rosie ran into his arms. Nadir raised the gun and fired. The weapon clicked harmlessly; Sahar had secretly bought blanks. Seeing the child untouched, Nadir dropped to his knees, believing she was an angel sent to save him.

Under a cold downpour on a rural road, Voss picked up a young man walking alone. They shared a quiet moment until the boy reached into his pocket. Voss misread the gesture, fired two rounds, and torched the cruiser to hide the body.

Detective Isaiah Reece was called to the roadside fire and stopped in his tracks, recognizing his brother Kwame’s shoes. When Reece broke the news, his mother collapsed on the kitchen floor, cursing Reece for never once looking for his brother.

At the Halstead home, Paula fell heavily down the stairs. She lay helpless until her housekeeper Alba found her, and in the ambulance, Paula confessed through tears that Alba was her only real friend.

Trey bought Pham’s abandoned van cheap at a garage. Expecting cargo, he opened the doors to find two dozen trafficked migrants locked in the dark. Trey drove them to the docks, handed them his pocket cash, and set them free.

As the year’s first snow began to fall, two cars collided at a busy city junction, and both drivers jumped out, shouting before even checking the damage.

In the house built for two, four adults, a baby, and a rottweiler named Tigre crowded the narrow rooms. Ruben slept on the couch, watching his brother Nestor’s wife, Alma, move across the kitchen. Nestor spent his nights robbing pharmacies under a scarf and his mornings knocking Alma across the room. Ruben urged her to run away with him, but words were not enough. When Ruben discovered Tigre killed other dogs on sight, he and his friend Pipo began entering him in underground pits. Tigre won steadily, and Ruben hid his earnings in the wardrobe to fund their escape. Desperate to speed things up, Ruben paid two thugs in a bar to beat Nestor. Nestor returned from the hospital, deduced Ruben’s hand in the assault within a day, and vanished with Alma, the baby, and every note Ruben had saved. Left with nothing but the fights, Ruben kept entering Tigre until promoter Chaco lost too much on a match and shot the dog in the ring. Ruben drove a knife into Chaco and fled in a truck with Pipo. Barreling through a red light at speed, Ruben crashed violently into a small turning car. Months later, when Nestor was shot dead robbing a bank, Ruben stood at the graveside and offered Alma escape one last time; she looked at him and refused.

Across the city, model Celine Vaz moved into a new flat facing a massive billboard carrying her own image. Her lover, Hector, had walked out on his wife and daughters at a birthday party to set her up in the high-rise. But after Ruben’s truck t-boned Celine’s car at the junction, she woke in a hospital ward, her leg bound in a steel cage of pins. Her lapdog, Chispa, was left trapped in the empty flat. Chispa fell through a hole in the floorboards, its faint whines rising through the gaps. While Hector obsessively tore up the floorboards with a crowbar searching for the dog, Celine’s leg went bad and turned gangrenous. Surgeons amputated her leg above the knee. That same week, workers stripped the billboard down, leaving Celine and Hector sitting in the wrecked flat, staring out at an empty frame.

At the crash site, Cardo—a former guerrilla turned vagrant hitman—pushed his scrap cart through the smoke. Ignoring the onlookers, he pulled the bleeding Tigre from the backseat and walked away. In a yard full of strays, Cardo nursed Tigre back to health over weeks, feeding the dog by hand until it slept beside him and followed him into the streets. Soon, a businessman named Elian met Cardo behind a church, handing him cash and a photograph to murder his half-brother and business partner, Sergio. Around that time, Cardo stood at the back of a cemetery watching his estranged wife’s burial—her mourners believing Cardo had been dead for twenty years—before following his grown daughter, Perla, home. Disaster struck when Cardo returned to his yard to find Tigre had slaughtered every other dog. Cardo pressed a gun barrel against the rottweiler’s head, but could not pull the trigger on the only thing he had saved. Instead of fulfilling the contract, Cardo snatched Sergio off the pavement and chained him to a bedframe in the empty yard. He then brought Elian there, sat the brothers face-to-face, laid a loaded pistol on the floor between them, and walked out having taken payment from both. Finally, Cardo broke into Perla’s flat while she was at work, left a long confession on her answering machine explaining who he was, took her photograph, and left all his money on her table. Shaved and dressed in clean clothes that did not fit, Cardo walked out into the flat grey wasteland at the edge of the city, Tigre trotting beside him.

Dressed as devout pilgrims, Solly Two Coats and his crew slipped through a northern port’s guarded showroom and walked out onto the misty docks with an extraordinary diamond. Across the sea, his cousin Marv placed a brief telephone call, ordering Solly to bring the stone over immediately. Instead, back in the city underworld, Grigor the Nail directed Solly toward a local bookmaker to place a wager, while secretly tipping off two bungling pawnbrokers, Ike and Benno, to rob him at the exact same location.

Across town, boxing promoters Halloway and Digby sent their contracted fighter, Pretty Sam, to buy a caravan at a travellers’ camp. An argument flared up, and Finn, an unheralded bare-knuckle fighter among the travellers, knocked Sam out cold with a single punch. Stranded without a man for gang boss Coldstone’s fixed bout, Halloway was forced to draft Finn into the ring, guaranteeing Coldstone that Finn would take a dive in the fourth round.

When Solly landed in the city, he quietly handed the diamond over to a fence named Hersch for safekeeping before heading to the bookmaker with an ostensibly prized carrying case. Inside the shop, Ike, Benno, and their partner Tulley completely bungled the robbery. They seized Solly by the arm and dragged him away along with his case, fleeing in panic when Grigor unexpectedly chased them off.

That night in the ring, Finn ignored his instructions entirely, knocking his opponent unconscious in the very first round. Coldstone lost a fortune on the bet and savagely took his anger out on Halloway. Flying into the city to investigate the delay, Marv found Solly gone and hired Ledge, a ruthless bounty hunter, to track down both his cousin and the missing stone.

Meanwhile, Grigor cornered Solly in a dark workshop and severed the man’s arm to force open the locked case, only to find it completely empty. Emlyn sat in Wilder’s sitting room late that evening, explaining with devastating calm that he had known about the affair for four full years. His wife had confessed the entire truth on a trip abroad, he said, adding with a faint, thin smile that he had never thought much of Wilder’s prose style in those intercepted letters either.

Only hours before that visit, Wilder had rung Emlyn in a state of wild panic, demanding his friend come to the house at once to face what had finally come to light.

The panic had taken root in a dimly lit bar, where Odile had carelessly let slip that Emlyn had recently agreed to publish a slick, second-rate novelist whom Wilder represented—a writer both men had quietly detested for years.

Just before dropping that detail in the bar, two years after their secret liaison had petered out, Odile had announced that her marriage was officially over. She told Wilder she had spent the previous night confessing every detail of their past affair to her husband, believing she was delivering a fresh blow.

Before that meeting, there had been the quiet, unceremonious liquidation of their shared domestic space. Wilder and Odile had systematically split their accumulated crockery and surrendered the lease on their rented rooms, not because they had been caught, but because the logistics of a second home had grown into a tedious chore.

Earlier still, over dinner at the married couple's dining table, Emlyn and Wilder had commandeered the entire evening, debating schoolboy sport and old racquet games with intense camaraderie until Odile was completely sidelined, possessing no part in the talk at all.

Prior to that dinner, Emlyn had pulled Wilder into a long, wine-soaked restaurant lunch. He spent the afternoon baiting his friend about the shortcomings of contemporary fiction, mocking his professional judgment while never once hinting at the revelation he was keeping to himself.

Before that lunch, Odile had returned to the quiet district directly from her travels. She spent the afternoon in the rented flat without saying anything whatever about the trip abroad, allowing the time to pass exactly as every other secret afternoon had passed.

Her reticence had been settled in a hotel room overseas, where she had confessed the betrayal in a rush of guilt, only for Emlyn to respond with chilling detachment, remarking that he had always been far fonder of his friend than of his wife.

That confession had been set off moments earlier in the hotel lobby, when Emlyn inquired about a message held for Odile at the reception desk, pointing out that the envelope was addressed in a hand he recognised at a glance.

Months before the journey abroad, Odile had sat on the edge of the secret bed and announced she was carrying her husband’s child, prompting the pair to decide that the rented rooms would continue precisely as they always had.

Before the pregnancy, they had found those rooms in a quiet district, stocking them with fine linen and matching plates to give their betrayal the anchor of an ordinary household.

And before any of it—before the lease, the plates, and the years of layered secrets—Wilder had taken Odile by the hand during a crowded party in his best friend’s house. While the other guests drank downstairs, he had led her into an upstairs room and told her how lovely she was.

A blinding beam weapon strikes him down at the lectern immediately after he finishes addressing a crowd, extinguishing his life in the exact manner he has always known it would end. On a planet far across the stars, inside a transparent zoo enclosure, alien captors exhibit him beside a famous film actress. The creature guides explain to him that every moment in time exists forever at once, and that free will is merely a comforting illusion peculiar to the confused inhabitants of Earth.

Confinement in a hospital ward brings him into contact with another patient, who introduces him to the endless paperback novels of a hack science fiction writer. He lies in the bed having suffered a total physical collapse shortly after returning home. In another place entirely, prisoners of war climb out from the subterranean meat locker of a disused city abattoir, stepping onto the street to discover that the surrounding metropolis has been utterly erased by a firestorm in a single night.

His daughter takes full control of his estate and daily affairs, convinced that his mind has finally succumbed to senility. She takes this step after he goes on a live radio talk show to describe his time in an alien zoo and lecture the listening audience on the true nature of the fourth dimension. Elsewhere in his life, he marries the daughter of an affluent man who owns a prosperous optometry school, inheriting a practice that makes him undeniably rich.

Down in the suffocating cellars beneath the burned city, captors force the surviving prisoners to dig thousands of bloated corpses out of the rubble, continuing the grim labor until one of the diggers dies on the spot from the dry heaves. It is within the prison system that an avenging prisoner looks at him and promises to have him killed one day to pay for the death of a scout. Long before or after, his father tosses him directly into the deep end of a public swimming pool to force him to learn to swim, but the weak, peculiar boy simply sinks to the concrete floor and lies there without struggling.

He survives a catastrophic air crash in the snowbound mountains, pulled from the burning debris by rescuers, yet his panicked wife dies from poisonous exhaust fumes while driving to the hospital to see him. On a packed prison train rolling through the cold, a scout dies of gangrene in a cattle car, spending his final moments blaming him for his death—the very scout who had previously beaten him in a frozen field behind enemy lines because he had begged to be left behind in the snow to die.

He begins life as a sickly, peculiar child born to modest parents in a dreary industrial town. Later or earlier, he is conscripted as a chaplain’s assistant and sent overseas on a transport ship without receiving any combat training worth mentioning. In an enemy prisoner camp, high-ranking officer captives live in extraordinary comfort, gorging themselves on double rations for years simply because an administrative clerical error was never corrected.
